Hearty Dried Pea Soup

Served at: Feast of the Ass

Serves 6-8Prep 20 minCook 1 hour 45 min

Dried Pea Soup, or 'pease pottage,' was a common and nourishing dish in medieval Europe, making it a fitting meal for the historical Feast of the Ass. This festival, celebrated in medieval times, often involved playful inversions of church rituals and honored the donkey's role in biblical narratives. A hearty bowl of pea soup would have provided warmth and sustenance to revelers during the cold winter months when this feast was typically observed.

Ingredients

  • 1 pound (450g) dried green split peas, rinsed
  • 8 cups (1.9 L) water or vegetable/chicken broth
  • 1 tablespoon (15ml) olive oil or butter
  • 1 large onion, chopped
  • 2 carrots, peeled and diced
  • 2 celery stalks, diced
  • 2 cloves garlic, minced
  • 1 smoked ham hock (about 1 pound/450g) or 4 ounces (113g) bacon, diced (optional, for traditional flavor)
  • 1 bay leaf
  • 1/2 teaspoon dried thyme
  • Salt and freshly ground black pepper to taste
  • Fresh parsley, chopped, for garnish (optional)

Method

  1. Rinse the dried split peas thoroughly under cold water. While split peas do not strictly require soaking, you may soak them for 2-4 hours to reduce cooking time slightly.
  2. In a large heavy-bottomed pot or Dutch oven, heat the olive oil or butter over medium heat. If using bacon, add it now and cook until crispy. Remove bacon with a slotted spoon and set aside, leaving the rendered fat in the pot.
  3. Add the chopped onion, carrots, and celery to the pot. Sauté for 8-10 minutes, or until the vegetables are softened and the onion is translucent.
  4. Add the minced garlic and cook for another minute until fragrant.
  5. Stir in the rinsed split peas, water or broth, ham hock (if using), bay leaf, and dried thyme.
  6. Bring the mixture to a boil, then reduce the heat to low, cover, and simmer for 1 hour 30 minutes to 1 hour 45 minutes, or until the peas are very tender and have started to break down, stirring occasionally to prevent sticking.
  7. If using a ham hock, carefully remove it from the pot. Once cool enough to handle, shred the meat from the bone and discard the bone and any excess fat. Return the shredded ham to the soup.
  8. Remove the bay leaf. Use an immersion blender to partially blend the soup for a creamier texture, leaving some whole peas for body, or mash with a potato masher. Alternatively, you can ladle a portion of the soup into a blender, blend, and return to the pot.
  9. Season the soup with salt and freshly ground black pepper to taste. Remember that ham or broth may already be salty.
  10. Ladle the hot soup into bowls. Garnish with fresh parsley and the reserved crispy bacon, if desired, before serving.

Tips

  • For a vegetarian version, simply omit the ham hock or bacon and use vegetable broth. You can add a pinch of smoked paprika for a hint of smoky flavor.
  • The soup thickens as it cools. If reheating, you may need to add a little extra water or broth to reach your desired consistency.
  • Serve with crusty bread for a complete and satisfying meal, true to its medieval roots.
